case_study_insert.main_stem: Vertex Apps (VAP) is a private limited company in the mobile-app and fintech sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2015 by Tomas Reyes, the firm develops mobile payment and loyalty apps for small independent retailers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. Vertex plans to invest $660,000 in a new mobile-payments platform, financed by a $360,000 bank loan and $300,000 venture capital. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.00 a unit and a selling price of $14.00, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. The firm faces two problems: rising user complaints about app crashes and a shortage of experienced developers.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Product Quality Report — Q1 2025: The payments app processed 250,000 transactions and shipped 14 release units last quarter, with a crash rate of 1.9%, down from 3.4% a year earlier. User complaints fell from 61 to 33 a month. Average app rating improved to 4.3 out of 5. A survey of 700 app users found 63% would pay up to $0.30 more for an ad-free version, and 58% value biometric security. A skills audit shows 16 of 55 developers need cloud-security training; courses cost $1,050 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Vertex Apps for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, raising the cost of variable-rate loans. (2) The minimum wage will increase by 6.5% from $12.90 to $13.74 an hour from April 2026. (3) Cloud server and third-party API input costs have risen 12.7% year-on-year, while digital payments transaction volume grew 8.4% and consumer inflation is 3.6%.

questions.question_text: VAP has funded its $660,000 mobile-payments platform with a $360,000 bank loan and $300,000 venture capital. Explain two advantages for VAP of using the $300,000 venture capital instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Venture capital requires no fixed interest or capital repayments, so Vertex avoids increasing the interest payable of 10 ($'000) and protects cash against fixed costs of $210,000 a year. With 70,000 units to sell and app-crash complaints to fix, the $300,000 lets Tomas Reyes invest fully in the $660,000 platform without squeezing the $7.00 contribution per unit to service debt.

Point 2: Venture capitalists bring sector expertise and contacts that a bank cannot, which can help a 55-person fintech improve its 1.9% crash rate and reach the 700 surveyed users. Unlike a larger loan, there is no repossession risk if launch volumes disappoint, although the investors will expect a share of ownership and a return on exit. The arrangement also spreads risk for a 55-person fintech with a 1.9% crash rate to fix: investor support can fund additional testing and the $1,050 training courses without forcing Vertex to cut the 70,000-unit plan or raise the $14.00 price prematurely.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: VAP is promoting its new mobile-payments platform. Consider app-store advertising, social-media influencer deals, or partnerships with retailer associations. Which should VAP choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
App-store advertising: Paid placements put the payments app in front of users actively downloading finance apps, with measurable installs and tight budget control, which suits a firm with fixed costs of $210,000. However, competition for prime keywords is expensive, installs do not guarantee active use, and the 1.9% crash rate would quickly undo any download gains.

Social-media influencer deals: Fintech and small-business influencers can demonstrate the app to the 63% of 700 users who would pay $0.30 more for an ad-free version and the 58% who value biometric security. This is targeted and relatively cheap but results are slower, depend on influencer credibility, and may attract users outside Vertex's independent-retailer base.

Partnerships with retailer associations: Working with bodies representing small independent retailers gives direct access to the firm's actual customers, builds trust and can be delivered through newsletters and events at low cost. The limits are a slower, relationship-led rollout and reliance on partners' willingness to promote a new platform. A further consideration is the app's 4.3 rating: partnerships with retailer associations can drive trials among real merchants whose feedback improves the product, whereas paid placements may simply add users who churn while the crash rate remains 1.9%.

Recommendation: VAP should choose partnerships with retailer associations, supported by modest app-store advertising. Associations reach the exact retailers the app serves, convert trust into usage and cost little, protecting the $300,000 venture capital. Influencer deals are rejected as too broad and slow, while app-store advertising alone is rejected as expensive and likely to generate installs that the 1.9% crash rate cannot retain.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of promotional options with minimal application to VAP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in VAP's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in VAP's context with a justified recommendation explaining why influencer deals and app-store advertising are rejected.

questions.question_text: Users have complained about app crashes at VAP. Explain two benefits for VAP of using democratic leadership to improve quality in its development team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites Vertex's developers to share ideas on fixing crashes, drawing on the people who know the code best and satisfying esteem needs (Maslow). Shared ownership should cut the 1.9% crash rate from 3.4% a year earlier and reduce user complaints from 61 to 33 a month, protecting the 4.3 app rating.

Point 2: Involving the 55-strong team in release decisions increases commitment and helps tackle the shortage of experienced developers by making the firm more attractive to work for. Better quality protects the $14.00 price and $7.00 contribution per unit, supports the $660,000 platform launch and reduces the need for further $1,050 training spending. Democratic leadership also suits the flat, 55-person structure, where developers can be given ownership of release quality without a layer of management slowing decisions. As the $660,000 platform scales, that involvement helps retain the experienced staff the firm currently lacks, protecting the 70,000-unit plan and the $300,000 venture capital investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: VAP must train 16 of its 55 developers in cloud security. Consider on-the-job mentoring or external courses costing $1,050 per employee. Which should VAP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job mentoring: Senior developers can coach the 16 staff on Vertex's own payments platform, which is directly relevant and costs no course fees, keeping the team productive while the $660,000 platform is launched. It supports the fall in crash rate to 1.9% and needs no time away from the 250,000 transactions processed. The limits are that mentors' own work suffers, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate, which the 58% of users valuing biometric security might expect.

External courses: Paying $1,050 per employee gives all 16 developers structured cloud-security skills and a recognised qualification, costing $16,800 in total — modest beside the $300,000 venture capital. The drawbacks are time away from development, delaying release units, and generic content that may not match Vertex's exact systems, so on-site follow-up would still be required. The choice also affects quality: the 1.9% crash rate must be reduced before the $660,000 platform can be marketed confidently, and in-house mentoring can address release-specific faults immediately, whereas a generic course cannot. With 250,000 transactions to support and only 55 developers, keeping staff on the product while they learn is a significant advantage, and the $16,800 course cost can be deferred until the platform stabilises.

Decision: VAP should choose on-the-job mentoring first, with external courses for the most senior developers. Mentoring is platform-specific, avoids the $16,800 outlay and disruption while the 1.9% crash rate must be fixed, and suits a 55-person flat team. Full external training is rejected because losing 16 developers during the platform launch would hurt the 70,000-unit target; courses can follow once releases stabilise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to VAP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in VAP's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in VAP's context with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VAP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Substitution: Break-even = $210,000 ÷ ($14.00 − $7.00) = $210,000 ÷ $7.00 = 30,000 units; margin of safety = 70,000 − 30,000 = 40,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 40,000 units.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.00 − $7.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VAP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. A margin of safety of 40,000 units above the 30,000 break-even point shows how far app-licence demand can fall before losses, guiding how much of the $360,000 loan to draw down.
2. Contribution per unit of $7.00 lets managers evaluate the survey finding that 63% of 700 users would pay $0.30 more for an ad-free version, lifting contribution to $7.30.
3. Fixed costs of $210,000 and $7.00 contribution set the volume needed to service the $360,000 loan and justify the $300,000 venture capital, so managers can test the 70,000-unit plan.
4. Average total cost of $10.00 ($210,000 ÷ 70,000 + $7.00) allows benchmarking against the 1.9% crash rate and 250,000 transactions, helping decide whether $1,050 training courses are worthwhile as API costs rise 12.7%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Margin of safety = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 30,000 break-even; $0.30 ad-free premium from the 700-user survey; servicing the $360,000 loan; unit-cost benchmarking at $10.00.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VAP's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed for 2024 and 2025. Which ratio gives the strongest evidence of improvement? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 38.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 44.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 11.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 16.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings (all figures $'000): 2024 gross margin = 304 ÷ 800 × 100 = 38.0%; 2025 = 440 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 44.0%. Operating return on sales 2024 = 88 ÷ 800 × 100 = 11.0%; 2025 = 160 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 16.0%. Return on capital 2024 = 88 ÷ 550 × 100 = 16.0%; 2025 = 160 ÷ 800 × 100 = 20.0%. Cost of sales rose from 496 to 560 while revenue grew from 800 to 1,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, so VAP's financial position has strengthened. The gross margin rising from 38.0% to 44.0% shows better control of direct costs even as server and API input costs rose 12.7%, and the operating return on sales climbing from 11.0% to 16.0% indicates the flat 55-person structure is absorbing overheads more effectively as revenue grows. Return on capital improved from 16.0% to 20.0%, meaning the 550 to 800 of capital employed — including the $300,000 venture capital — is working harder. The strongest evidence is the 16.0-point rise in operating return on sales, because it shows a large, sustained improvement in profitability from operations rather than a figure flattered by the enlarged capital base. A caveat is interest payable rising from 10 to 12 as the $360,000 loan is serviced.

Conclusion: VAP's financial position has improved on all three measures. The sharp lift in operating return on sales from 11.0% to 16.0% is the clearest evidence of underlying progress; the small rise in loan interest is the main risk to monitor.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of cost, revenue and capital movements, and a justified conclusion naming the strongest evidence.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VAP of adding biometric login to its payments app.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Biometric login directly meets the survey finding that 58% of 700 users value biometric security, strengthening trust in the $660,000 payments platform and supporting the $14.00 price and $7.00 contribution per unit. It also reinforces the 63% willing to pay $0.30 more for an ad-free version and helps lift the 4.3 app rating while reducing complaint-driven churn among 55-staff operations.

Disadvantage: Implementing biometrics adds development cost on top of fixed costs of $210,000 and competes with the urgent need to cut the 1.9% crash rate, potentially delaying releases. With 16 of 55 developers needing cloud-security training and a 6.5% minimum wage rise, the extra security work may raise the $7.00 variable cost and squeeze margins before the $360,000 loan is serviced. Tomas Reyes should sequence the biometric work after the crash-rate fixes, using the 700-user survey to prioritise features, so that the $660,000 platform launches reliably and the 4.3 rating is protected.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 12.7% rise in cloud server input costs will affect VAP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If VAP's $360,000 loan is variable-rate, the extra 0.75% costs 0.75% × $360,000 = $2,700 a year — small against fixed costs of $210,000 and interest payable of 12 ($'000). If the loan is fixed, the direct effect is nil. Higher rates could raise the cost of future borrowing for the $660,000 platform, but fixing the rate would largely remove this risk.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.74 an hour): The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The defensible judgement is qualitative: with a workforce of 55, a compulsory rise pushes up costs that cannot be avoided and squeezes the $7.00 contribution per unit unless productivity or the $14.00 price rises; the 63% of users willing to pay $0.30 more for ad-free access offers partial recovery.

Cloud server input costs (12.7%): Vertex's $7.00 variable cost is affected by servers and APIs, but the insert never decomposes it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $7.00 rose 12.7%, that is 12.7% × $7.00 = $0.89 per unit, and at 70,000 units about $62,300 a year. Even a $0.30 rise would cost $21,000 a year, cutting contribution toward $6.70 and threatening the app's 4.3 rating as performance suffers.

Conclusion: The 12.7% rise in cloud server input costs will have the greatest impact because it applies to every one of the 70,000 units and directly erodes the contribution that funds the $660,000 platform. The wage rise is important but not quantifiable from the insert, and the roughly $2,700 interest effect is small; VAP should renegotiate server contracts and pursue the $0.30 ad-free premium.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VAP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
